title: The Hawk, the Kite, and the Pigeons
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: The Pigeons in a certain dovecote were persecuted by a Kite, who every now and then swooped down and carried off one of their number. So they invited a Hawk into the dovecote to defend them against their enemy. But they soon repented of their folly: for the Hawk killed more of them in a day than the Kite had done in a year.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who was persecuting the Pigeons in the dovecote?
options: A Kite
A Fox
An Owl
A Cat

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Kite do every now and then?
options: Swooped down and carried off one of their number
Circled overhead without attacking
Built a nest inside the dovecote
Stole grain from a nearby farm

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who did the Pigeons invite into the dovecote?
options: A Hawk
An Eagle
A larger flock of pigeons
A farmer

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did the Pigeons invite the Hawk in?
options: To defend them against their enemy
To teach them how to fly faster
To help them build a bigger dovecote
To scare away the farmer

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the Hawk's harm to the Pigeons compare with the Kite's?
options: The Hawk killed more of them in a day than the Kite had done in a year
The Hawk killed exactly as many as the Kite each year
The Hawk never killed any pigeons at all
The Hawk only killed pigeons that strayed outside the dovecote

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "persecuted" mean in "were persecuted by a Kite"?
options: Repeatedly harassed or attacked
Politely visited
Closely studied
Warmly welcomed

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the Pigeons come to regret inviting the Hawk?
options: The protector they chose turned out to be far more dangerous than the enemy it was meant to stop
The Hawk refused to stay in the dovecote for very long
The Kite returned and drove the Hawk away
The Hawk demanded payment the Pigeons could not afford

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Kites are always weaker than hawks
Turning to a more dangerous power for protection can bring greater harm than the original threat
Dovecotes should never be built near open fields
Pigeons are incapable of defending themselves

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where did the Pigeons live?
options: In a certain dovecote
In a tall barn
In a hollow tree
In an open field

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what feeling did the Pigeons have once the Hawk moved in?
options: They soon repented of their folly
They felt completely safe at last
They were indifferent to the change
They celebrated their clever plan

questions.prompt: According to the passage, over what span of time had the Kite been carrying off pigeons?
options: A single day
A year
A week
An hour

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "folly" mean in "they soon repented of their folly"?
options: A foolish or unwise action
A joyful celebration
A long journey
A formal agreement

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what mistake did the Pigeons make in choosing the Hawk as their defender?
options: They trusted a predator, assuming it would treat them better than their existing enemy did
They chose an animal too small to fight off the Kite
They forgot to ask the Hawk to leave once the Kite was gone
They failed to warn the Hawk about the Kite at all

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: The Pigeons defeat the Kite on their own without any outside help
The Pigeons invite a Hawk to protect them from a Kite, only to have the Hawk harm them far more
The Kite and the Hawk join forces against the Pigeons
The Hawk drives the Kite away and then leaves the Pigeons in peace
